title: Goals in life
goal: Setting goals helps couples strengthen their relationship as they then work together as a team towards a common aim. It can help you understand what is really important to you and to your partner, and having a common goal can help you to stick together, even during the most challenging times. It is about moving toward what you want, not necessarily achieving it. However, if you reach your goal, then don’t forget to celebrate together!
howTo:
Take a moment to imagine your life in the future, and focus specifically on your relationship. Think about where you want to be and what you want to do in the next six months to two years. Next imagine where you want your lives to be in five, ten and twenty years. Start making a list of practical and shoot-for-the-moon goals. Difficulties starting?

When you have both finished your lists of goals it’s time to prioritize and get specific about how you will achieve these goals together. Keep it positive and don't criticize any ideas until you've had the chance to get them on the table first. Setting goals as a couple is as much about strengthening your bond as it is about achieving your actual goals.

questions.question: Ask yourself what values are important to me, to my relationship.
questions.description: Think of a bucket list of things you would like to do on your own, with your partner or with family or friends.

questions.question: Imagine you bump into a friend 5 years from now.

title: What is your love language?
goal:
Discover your love language and your partners love language. You come to understand how you experience love and to realise that you are most likely to express your love for another in the same way as you prefer to experience it yourself.

You might have heard of ‘The Five Love Languages’ by Dr. Gary Chapman. His first book on this subject was published in 1995 and has been consistently on the New York Times Best Seller list. Chapman holds that there are five main ways that people show their affection; this also tends to be the way they prefer to receive affection too: Words of Affirmation, Quality Time, Physical Touch, Acts of Service and Gifts.

Some people feel loved when their partner brings them a coffee in the morning: This is a great example of Act of Service.


Some need their partner to tell them how good they look or how well they handled something: These are words of Affirmation.


Some people always buy their partner a present if they’ve been away: Obviously this is Gifts.


Others require physical forms of affection such as a kiss or stroke through the hair: These are expressions of “Physical Touch”.
howTo:
You and your partner separately do a test to discover your love language.

1. Below you will find 30 questions with two statements each. Select the statement that you prefer most. It is the one that fits the best right now.


2. Talk about your love language and think about your own needs and your partner’s.

title: Active listening
goal:
Relationships are all about communication. Sometimes it happens that we listen to our partners speaking without really hearing what they are saying. This means we miss opportunities to connect with our partners – and even worse – risk making them feel neglected, disrespected, and resentful. In order to avoid this, the two of you are going to experiment with active listening.

This exercise helps you both express active interest in what your partner has to say and to make him or her feel heard so as to foster empathy and connection. Active listening creates a safe space in which one's thoughts and feelings do not come under judgment. This is crucial in a relationship, as you want to be able to talk freely and openly to each other.
howTo:
Find a quiet place where you can talk with your partner without interruption or distraction. Invite them to share what’s on their mind. When they do so, try to follow the steps below. You don’t need to cover every step, but the more you do cover, the more effective this exercise is likely to be.

1. Sit facing each other

2. Set a timer for 5 minutes

3. Just talk about whatever you feel like talking about: What has been on your mind lately, how do you feel about your partner.....whatever you feel you would like to talk about.

4. Use engaged body language. Show that you are interested by maintaining eye contact, and try to maintain eye contact with them the entire time.

5. Express empathy. If the other person voices negative feelings, strive to validate these feelings rather than questioning or defending against them. For example, if the speaker expresses frustration, try to consider why he or she feels that way, regardless of whether you think that feeling is justified or whether you would feel that way yourself were you in his or her position. 

6. Avoid judgment. Your goal is to understand the other person’s perspective and accept it for what it is, even if you disagree with it. Try not to interrupt with counter-arguments or mentally prepare a rebuttal while the other person is speaking.

7.Avoid giving advice. Problem-solving is likely to be more effective once you understand your partner’s perspective and when they feel heard. Moving too quickly into advice-giving can be counterproductive. 

Did you finish the exercise?

Take turns so once the timer has gone off, the roles switch and the other partner has their turn to speak in an uninterrupted stream of consciousness.

title: Let's talk about sex
goal: In the early seventies, it was believed that only men had sexual fantasies. We nowadays know better and having sexual fantasies, whether you want to act them out or not, is completely natural and healthy. A 2001 study in the Journal of Sex Research found that 98% of men and 80% of women had fantasized about someone other than their partner in the previous 2 months! However, how to talk to your partner about sex can be one of the more challenging aspects of a relationship. Without being able to truly communicate about sex there is a danger that people engage in sexual activities they don’t really enjoy. Sexual satisfaction depends on your ability to express what arouses or interests you and what doesn’t.
howTo:
How do you talk with each other about sex?

Here are some pointers to get you started:

1. Make sure that you and your partner are ready to discuss this topic. Timing can make a huge difference in how and where a sexual conversation goes. Pick a time when you have some privacy and are not rushed, so you can both think about what’s being said and how it feels before you respond. Great if that can happen today, but its absolutely fine if you decide together to do this exercise another day.

2. Agree on confidentiality. Whenever you bring up a new sexual conversation with your partner, you are exposing a part of yourself and you need to feel safe.

3. You can start by asking each other questions about where you most like to be touched, what you liked best the last time you made love, what is your favourite place to kiss your partner’s body, what makes sex more exciting for you, do you have a fantasy you would like to share, is there a special love toy you’d like to try and what about watching erotic movies together?

Try what works for you. Things that are new can feel uncomfortable or awkward at first, and having a sense of humour can help. There is no right or wrong, just have fun with discovering your sexual communication and see what happens. It's a nice idea to end your conversation sharing at least one positive thing that came out of it.

You can record it and send it to your partner at a moment you want to surprise him or her with a sex date.

title: Expressing gratitude
goal:
Expressing gratitude improves our physical and mental health as well as our relationships.

Praise each other and show your appreciation for each other by writing the other one a letter.
howTo:
1. Set a timer for 15 minutes

2. Take a piece of paper and write a letter expressing the gratitude you feel for the other.

Try using the following as a guide:

Address your partner directly, “Dear ______”.

Don’t worry about perfect grammar or spelling.

Describe in specific terms something your partner does or has done, why you are grateful for that, and how his/her behavior affected your life. Try to use a concrete example. Describe what you are doing in your life now and how you often remember his or her efforts. Try to keep your letter to roughly one page (~300 words). If you find it difficult, you can start writing a list of things you really like about your partner. You could start by praising some aspect of your partner’s character, then their accomplishments, or anything else that comes to mind. There are no restrictions on what you are or are not allowed to write. Everything is ok.

3. If you don’t manage to finish the letter today, finish it another time. Make sure you agree on a special moment when you will give each other the letters.﻿

goal: Connect by indulging in a sensual spoiling session. A spoiling session is an exercise that allows you to gain a deeper understanding of your own sexual needs and the sexual needs of your partner, while simultaneously reconnecting you as a couple and melting away the subtle shame and resistance that each partner may or may not have towards sex in general. Free of any expectations.
howTo:
1. Decide which partner will be first and also decide the amount of time you will share together. On day 12 there is another ‘sensual spoiling session’ when the other partner will enjoy the experience of being sensually spoiled for the same amount of time.

2. Role play. The partner who goes first is Lover A, and the other partner is

Lover B.

Lover A guides Lover B, expressing his/her desires and fantasies.

Lover B will be the listener.

3. Preparations Lover A: put together your intimate sensual spoiling box: The ideal size is probably a shoe box, or something a little smaller.  Fill this spoiling box with inventive toys such as feathers, flowers, straws, shells, crystals, leaves, sticks, necklaces, brushes, musical instruments such bells/ tingshas /a singing bowl, maybe food like grapes, strawberries, peanut butter, chocolate spread, or massage oils/ fragrances, ice cubes. Go for things you can imagine your lover using to tickle, kiss, squeeze, scratch, wipe, push, drip, blow, stroke, slap, sprinkle, rub and tap all over your body.

Lover A.

You are vulnerable, You are strong, You guide your lover.

You initiate how, where and with what your lover can touch you. 

You can choose to start with a slow gentle full body massage or maybe a strong shoulder massage. 

You are in charge; you take the decisions. You could invite your lover to use their hand(s), finger(s), toe(s), elbow(s), nose, mouth, tongue, belly, bump and/or any of the extras from your intimate spoiling box.

Lover A is welcoming the inner creativity of being the master, of sharing their inner sensuality and is active in exploring playfulness and boundaries.


Lover B.

You are the listener. The non-judgmental listener.

You are vulnerable: by being curious and friendly. 

You are strong: by being passive.

You are open to all the sensual invitations from Lover A.

IMPORTANT FOR BOTH LOVERS: Be present! 

Surrender to the moment; be in the moment.  Both of you are patient and respectful, practice a non-judgmental awareness. Be aware of each others do’s and don’ts, the yes or the no.

title: Non-Violent Communication (NVC)
goal: According to Marshall Rosenberg, conflicts often arise because we do not understand each other’s needs. Do you know the needs of your partner? If you and your partner use the language of compassion it could help to shift this aspect of your relationship.
howTo:
Think of a moment when you were really annoyed with your partner.

Use the form set out below the exercise to write it down, or just give your partner an example by following 4 steps:

observation, feelings, need and request.

OBSERVATION: Describe what happened at the moment you were annoyed. Use words like ‘ what I see, notice, hear, observe, etc

For example: What I observe is that you are on your phone the whole time when I am talking to you.

FEELINGS: Describe how you felt about it?

For example: I felt neglected.

NEEDS: Tell your partner what your needs are in this particular case.

For example: I want to be heard.

REQUEST: what is it that you want from him or her and ask this.

For example: Can you please put the phone aside when we have a conversation?

Summarize what it is you want to say to your partner without judging him or her. In our example this could go something like, “When I see you busy with your phone whilst I’m telling you a story, I feel neglected, I want to be heard. Are you willing to put the phone aside whilst we have a conversation?”

Over the coming days you can experience what happens when you try addressing your partner using the language of compassion.

When your partner says something to you that you didn’t like hearing, try to also follow the four steps.
background: Marshall B. Rosenberg, Ph.D. (1934-2015) is an American psychologist who developed in the 1960’s the Nonviolent Communication, also described as a language of compassion, a tool for social change. He founded and was for many years the Director of Educational Services for the Center for Nonviolent Communication, an international peacemaking organization. His bestselling book Nonviolent Communication: A Language of Life has sold more than one million copies worldwide and has been translated into more than 30 languages. Play Video

title: A trip down memory lane
goal:
You will be taking a walk down memory lane. Whether you and your partner have only been together for a few months, or for years or decades, you are bound to have incredible memories.

This exercise encourages you both to focus on your shared positive and or life changing moments.

The purpose of this exercise is twofold: First, it will reinforce the realisation that you and your partner have shared many positive moments and remembering these can create a more positive feeling about your relationship. Second, by reinforcing positive memories you are much more likely to create more positive memories.
howTo: Record your song and then upload it. Take a photo of your relationship symbol and upload that, together with your photo of your before and after moment. You need these three items for tomorrow’s exercise.

questions.question: Choose a song
questions.description: Choose a song that reminds you of the moment you first noticed your partner or one that has a special meaning for you both.

questions.question: Find a photo
questions.description: Find a photo that reminds you of a ‘before and after moment’, that’s the moment when your world would never be the same again. Try to find an image that will pave your memory lane.

questions.question: Find an object
questions.description: Find an object that is the essence of now, an artefact or symbol of the current dominating force in your relationship. It can be a souvenir from one of your recent holidays or something you now use every day. Something that features in your relationship right now.

title: The Story of Us: Part 1
goal:
Our stories come from our memories and experiences; they are the framework we use to integrate the pivotal events in our lives. Our stories help us to understand and give meaning to our lives. In a sense, we become the stories we tell ourselves.

This exercise is designed to shine light on your relationship story to increase your awareness of the subconscious energy influencing your relationship, and to open the possibility of authoring your future relationship stories.

Today Kinchem, the creator of this exercise, will explain how to do the exercise herself.
howTo:
Individually answer a series of questions to help you compose your version of your relationship story. When you have written your ‘story of us’ you’ll take turns, on day 21 to read, tell, or show it to your partner. You’ll only have 5 minutes to read or tell your story to your partner, so make sure you practise your timing. You need to make choices about what is included in the story, and what isn’t. Ask yourself what elements of your story currently have the biggest impact on your relationship. To do this exercise you will need the three relationship symbols you collected in the previous exercise:

  • 1. Song, That reminds you of the moment you first noticed your partner.
  • 2. Photo, That reminds you of the moment of ‘before and after’, when your world would never be the same again
  • 3. Object, That is the essence of now, an artefact or symbol of the current dominating force in your relationship
background: Kinchem Hegedus , a writer from Australia, will now guide you and your partner in this process. Kinchem Hegedus lives and works in Sydney with her family and she organizes courses that help you with mapping your “inner landscape”.

title: Rituals
goal:
Rituals of connection are shared activities that you do on a repeated basis from daily to yearly that have meaning for you as a couple. Research shows that what makes a relationship successful are small things done often. Rituals connect us with others by providing a focus or activity that enables us to interact in an enjoyable and meaningful way.

For example, some couples have a daily routine of checking in with each other by phone at some point during the day. It only becomes a ritual, though, if it is used as a moment to connect rather than just an exercise in exchanging information.

Just like our essential daily vitamins, a number of simple rituals can keep our relationships healthy and vibrant.
howTo:
Create your own ritual list. It’s possible you already have numerous ‘couple rituals’ and you aren’t even aware of them. It may be that after today you choose a couple ritual that you would like to build into your relationship.

What are some of the couple rituals you have?  What aspects make them meaningful and significant to you? How can you modify your ritual to make it more effective?

Talk about these rituals together and identify why certain rituals are important to you.

Maybe consider how these rituals played out in your childhood home – have you adopted one or adapted it, or is it something you two have created for yourselves?

Below the exercise you will find a drop down menu giving a list of rituals. Take a moment to select the ones you wish to talk about with your partner.

Have fun with it.

Spending a morning in bed talking or cuddling
Calling or texting just to check-in during the day
Setting up a specific time of day to talk and catch up
Holding each others’ hands (while walking, watching tv, etc)
Celebrating special days or important days (birthdays, anniversaries, etc.)
Taking care of one another when sick
Renewing your commitment to each other on your anniversary
Attending concerts, plays, and other cultural events
Attending a partner’s performance or sports event
Participating in community events or politics
Apologizing or repairing feelings after an argument

title: The Melting Hug
goal:
Multiple studies show that human touch triggers the release of the hormone “oxytocin” in our brain and reduces the stress hormone, “cortisol”.

Oxytocin gives us a sense of connection and bonding. This so called-love hormone is a neurotransmitter that increases feelings of trust, generosity and compassion, and decreases feelings of fear and anxiety.

When our cortisol levels are high, our skin actually gets more sensitive, so the healing touch of your partner’s hand is most effective when stress levels are highest. The reduction of cortisol is beneficial for the heart, circulatory system, and brain. Essentially, holding hands can make you healthier!
howTo:
The Melting Hug: hug through your breath, both of you breathing in a synchronistic, unifying way.

  • 1. Set the timer for 3 minutes
  • 2. Stand in front of your partner and touch each other, nestle against your partner’s chest; slowly wrap your arms gently around each other. Let your hands feel they are really holding flesh, bones, and muscles without exerting pressure. Embrace the whole body don’t just squeeze each other.
  • 3. Let your pelvis relax and move forward, rest against each other pelvis to pelvis. Allow your thighs and bellies to meet. Keep your knees slightly bent to enhance your sense of balance and groundedness. Let your bodies relax so that you can melt into each other, give yourselves over to a trusting embrace. Feel secure; welcome the same sensation of letting-go that a child feels in its mother's embrace.
  • 4. Start to take notice of your partner’s breathing pattern. Let your own breathing harmonize with your partner’s so that you softly inhale and exhale together. If this harmonized breathing comes easily, enjoy the feeling and relax into it for a few minutes or take three full breathes, inhaling and exhaling together. You need not make any effort and shouldn’t feel any tension. In this exercise, you welcome, receive and dissolve into each other.
background: Margot Anand (1944) is an internationally acclaimed authority on Tantra, best-selling author, and much-beloved teacher and founder of SkyDancing Tantra®. She lives on Bali and USA. www.margotanand.com.

title: Where do we stand?
goal:
You and you partner will discover how emotionally responsive you are by doing an exercise based on Emotional Focussed Therapy: EFT. Dr. Sue Johnson is the primary developer of Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy, which has demonstrated its effectiveness in over 25 years of peer- reviewed clinical research. The message of EFT is simple: Recognize and admit that you are emotionally attached to and dependent on your partner in much the same way that a child is on a parent for nurturing, soothing, and protection.

In secure love relationships, partners experience the other person as:

1. Accessible, which means I can count on my partner, he or she feels near and I can reach him or her;

2. Responsive, which means when I ask for help or connection, I can get it;

3. And Engaged, which means my partner is really interested in me and wants to grow our love.
howTo: Please go through the list of statements and answer whether you feel this is “True” or “False” in your relationship. Once you have gone through the list award 1 point for all the statements that you feel are “True”. If your score is 7 or higher, you are on the right track. If your score is below 7 points, it may be helpful to extend this exercise by talking to your partner about the answers each of you gave. Were they similar? Are you experiencing the same issues? Use the active listening method when discussing your answers and try to understand why your partner answered the way he/she did.

content.subtitle: From your viewpoint, is your partner accessible to you?

list.text: I can get my partner’s attention easily.
My partner is easy to connect with emotionally.
My partner shows me that I come first with him/her.
I am not feeling lonely or shut out in this relationship
I can share my deepest feelings with my partner. He/she will listen.

content.subtitle: From your viewpoint is your partner responsive to you?

list.text: If I need connection and comfort, he/she will be there for me.
My partner responds to signals that I need him/her to come close.
I find I can lean on my partner when I am anxious or unsure.
Even when we fight or disagree, I know that I am important to my partner and we will find a way to come together.
If I need reassurance about how important I am to my partner, I can get it.

content.subtitle: Are you positively emotionally engaged with each other?

list.text: I feel very comfortable being close to, trusting my partner.
I can confide in my partner about almost anything.
I feel confident, even when we are apart, that we are connected to each other.
I know that my partner cares about my joys, hurts, and fears.
I feel safe enough to take emotional risks with my partner.

data.description: Take this questionnaire twice. The first time round you should answer the 15 questions about your partner, about how Accessible, Responsive, and Engaged your partner is with you. The second time you answer the questions, do so about yourself. focusing on how Accessible, Responsive, and Engaged you are towards your partner.

background: Dr. Sue Johnson is an author, clinical psychologist, researcher, professor and a leading innovator in the field of couple therapy. Sue is the primary developer of Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy (EFT), which has demonstrated its effectiveness in over 25 years of peer-reviewed clinical research. Her best-selling book Hold me Tight has been translated in 22 languages. She lives in Ottawa, Canada, with her husband and two children.

title: Values of life
goal:
Extensive research into the qualities of a happy couples has concluded that the most important element of a long-lasting, loving relationship is a shared attitude to life.

This means that one of the reasons why happy couples work so well together, despite being quite different people, is because there is a deeper level of shared values that keeps them solid and maybe surprisingly compatible.

Our values play a role in many aspects of our life including the choices we make, how we react or respond to situations, who we spend time with, the boundaries we set, and so much more. When our values are being honoured, we feel good. You and your partner will discover and discuss your values in life.
howTo:
• 1. Go through the list of 35 Value Questions.
  • 2. Check up to 10 values that are most important to you.
  • 3. Rank them in importance from 1-10.
  • 4. Discuss the values when you have both finished. Why did you choose these? What do you mean by a particular value?
  • 5. Choose at least 5 values which you both agree will be “Your values in life”.
  • 6. Make a photo and hang it up somewhere in your home so you see them every day! When you know what you believe in, it’s so much easier to make decisions that are in line with the kind of life you want to live.

title: Love Map
goal: Create your own love map by playing “ The Love Map game’. The principle behind building a Love Map is simply: knowing the little things about your partner’s life creates a strong foundation for your friendship and intimacy. Research has found that emotionally intelligent couples are intimately familiar with each other’s worlds. They know each other’s goals in life, each other’s worries, each other’s hopes and dreams. Without such a love map, you can’t really know your partner. It is said that couples who have detailed love maps of each other’s world are far better prepared to cope with stressful events and conflict.
howTo:
• 1. Write the numbers 1 through 20 on a piece of paper. Then take turns asking your partner the questions below.
  • 2. If your partner answers correctly (and YOU are the judge), he or she receives the number of points indicated for that question, and you also receive one point. If your partner answers incorrectly, neither of you receives any points. High score wins.

  • While you’re having fun playing, you’ll also be expanding and deepening your relationship.

The Love Map

Name my two closest friends. (2)
What was I wearing when we first met? (2)
Name one of my hobbies. (3)
What stresses am I facing right now? (4)
Describe in detail what I did today, or yesterday. (4)
What kind of present would I like best? (2)
What personal improvements do I want to make in my life? (4)
What was my favourite holiday? (2)
What is one of my greatest fears or disaster scenarios? (3)
What is my favourite restaurant? (2)
What turns me on sexually? (3)
What is my favourite time of the day for lovemaking? (2)
Of all the people we both know, who do I like the least? (3)
What is my favourite TV show? (2)
Do I have a secret ambition? What is it? (4)
What was my worst childhood experience? (3)
What is the date of our anniversary? (1)
Who is my greatest source of support (other than you)? (3)
What are the important events coming up in my life? How do I feel about them? (4)
What is one of my favourite ways to spend an evening? (2)
background: Dr. John Gottmann (1942) is a professor emeritus in psychology known for his work on marital stability and relationship analysis through scientific direct observations. In his book, The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work, he sets out his idea for building a Love Map. With his wife, Julie Schwartz, Gottman heads a non-profit research institute (The Relationship Research Institute) and a for-profit therapist training entity (The Gottman Institute). www.gottman.com
